speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next week the World Food Council will be meeting in Rome for its annual meeting. It has been a tradition in this UN body that the immediate past president of the Council is invited to this meeting. The Hon. Eugene Whelan was involved in the founding of this Council in 1974 and represented Canada at its meetings with distinction almost every year since. He has not only represented the region of Canada, the United States and western Europe on the Council, but has also served on the Bureau, which is the executive committee. In 1985 he completed a two-year term as President of the World Food Council.
His experience and knowledge of world food problems would be invaluable to the Council at its meeting next week. I find it strange that Mr. Whelan has not been invited to attend this meeting in his capacity as immediate past president. Is this an oversight, or an example of a mean-spirited Government? I call on the Government to ensure that Mr. Whelan takes his rightful place at this meeting of the World Food Council.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-DENIAL OF PASSPORT TO WINNIE MANDELA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Winnie Mandela has been denied a passport by the South African Government that would have enabled her to travel to Peru this month to attend the Congress of Socialist International Women. This is yet one more example of the total lack of freedom and basic human rights for the vast majority of people living in South Africa.
Like countless black men and women, Winnie Mandela is denied not only the freedom to speak and basic freedoms of political action in her own country, but she and they are denied the opportunity to practise such freedoms outside South Africa. The Botha government has now rejected the measures proposed by the Eminent Persons Group. It is time for Canada
to show some leadership in pressing for urgent change in South Africa. It is time for real economic sanctions.

subsubtopic: IMPORTANCE OF ESTABLISHING EFFICIENT NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity to participate in the National Conference on Scientific and Technological Policy which ended yesterday in Winnipeg. In attendance at the conference were representatives of industry and of the Science Council, researchers in various fields, academics, union members, as well as federal and provincial Ministers. On the basis of a working document, the purpose of this forum was to study the situation and seek the views of all participants so as to lay the foundation of a productive national policy on science and technology. They all made constructive contributions and showed keen interest in the proceedings, for they are all aware that such a policy will have an impact on the future of our country.

subsubtopic: CONFERENCE DISCUSSION OF NATIONAL SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 9 and 10 I attended a forum in Winnipeg hosted by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle). It was attended by leading Canadians from business, government, labour, and universities, who are interested in science and technology. Its purpose was to debate the need for, and essentials of, a national science policy for Canada. This objective was unanimously endorsed.
Other endorsements included the recognition of the fundamental importance of research and technology to our economic and cultural development, the need for more support for basic and applied research, the importance of science in all levels of education, and the importance of technology transfer to small business. It was an historic and exciting occasion and

June 11, 1986
a resounding success, a splendid example of the Government's commitment to consultation and leadership.

Yesterday and last night a severe storm destroyed the lobster and fishing gear of hundreds of fishermen in that area.
I want to call upon the Government, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), to undertake immediately in conjunction with the Minister of Fisheries for Newfoundland, an assessment of the damage to the fishery in that area and to work with the local fishermen's organizations to provide the necessary infrastructure to allow those fishermen to go back to work as soon as possible.
This time of year is crucial to a successful fishery. The fishermen will not be able to support their families unless quick action is taken. I ask the Government to consider the matter as quickly as possible.

subsubtopic: NECESSITY FOR GOVERNMENT TO HELP BLUEBERRY PRODUCERS' CO-OPERATIVES IN LAC-SAINT-JEAN REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week private producers and co-operatives in the Lac-Saint-Jean area lost most of their blueberry crop to spring frost, which could result in a loss of income of as much as $3 million.
According to Mr. Joseph Savard, as quoted in La Presse, the harvest will be almost a total loss, and last week's spring frost was the worst on record for the area.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) must help these producers who have no crop insurance and who are in an area that already has an unemployment rate of 17 per cent.

subsubtopic: INVITATION TO ATTEND WORLD FOLKLORE FESTIVAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to invite all Hon. Members and all Canadians to come to the riding of Drummond this summer for the Fifth World Folklore Festival to be held from July 4 to July 14. About half a million visitors are expected.
For ten days, the Festival will host more than 40 folk dance groups from all over the world, including Australia, the United States, France, Hungary and the Soviet Union, and Canadian participants from Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia.
These groups will demonstrate the folk culture of various countries through their songs, music, dance and a host of fascinating activities.
This unique festival offers a broad range of activities in a program worthy of major international events, including ceremonies on a grand scale, concerts, community activities, a torch-lit procession, Fire works and a folkoteque. I again invite you all to come and discover the traditions of this country and from countries all over the world.

subsubtopic: POSITIONS OF OPPOSITION PARTIES ON TRADE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while on the international trade front the Conservative Government resolutely defends the interests of Canadian workers and staunchly promotes expanding markets for Canadian products, the NDP typically pulls its horns into its shell and pretends
June 11, 1986

that the world does not exist. What is difficult to understand, however, is the complete absence of any policy on the part of the Liberals. They appear to be mired down in a morass of confusion and internal conflict.
When will the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) get off the fence? Will he throw in his lot with the pussy-footing protectionist from Winnipeg-Fort Garry or the fiscalamitous free trader from Saint-Henri-Westmount? Or is he just too busy looking over his shoulder trying to find out what Jean Chretien is up to?

subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR GOVERNMENT TO REVIEW ITS POSITION CONCERNING THE ELDERLY
speechtext:
Over the last weekend, Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege to meet representatives of senior citizens who were simply asking, what do the Prime Minister and this Conservative Government have against the aged?
Over the past 20 months, there have been 5 measures detrimental to senior citizens. There was first the discrimination in connection with the spouse allowance; then the deindexing of old age security pensions; then the unemployment insurance benefit cuts in the case of workers having elected early retirement; finally, the rejection of all Job Development projects involving home-cleaning services for the aged. And we learn now about the cuts in the order of $3 million made to the New Horizons Programs directed at senior citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that during the meeting of the Cabinet priority Committee, the Government will review its position and improve its image with senior citizens by granting them what they deserve. These people have worked all their lives for the benefit of Canada.

speechtext:

Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) recognized the unjust and unfair treatment by this policy of the western Canadian oil industry and the people of western Canada.
Oral Questions
As a result, one of the first acts of our Government was the signing of the Western Accord which dismantled the hated national energy policy. The Western Accord calls for the phasing out by 1988 of the unfair production tax. speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN AND THE FEDERAL COURT
speechtext:
that Bill C-116, an Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan and the Federal Court Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pride to bring forward legislation entitled an Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan and the Federal Court Act, Bill C-116. It is the culmination of several years of consultation and co-operation among Canadians on the subject of pension reform.
The amendments to the Canada Pension Plan which we are discussing today will have far-reaching implications for virtually all Canadians in the labour force and for their families. As well, they will implement significant improvements for many individuals who are already receiving benefits under the plan. Indeed, there are few Canadians who will not benefit from the reforms to the Canada Pension Plan which are proposed to come into effect on January 1, 1987.1 believe I can state that this legislation is one of the most important Bills that the Government will introduce during its present mandate. Twenty-five years from now many of the issues that have preoccupied both sides of this House will undoubtedly have faded to the dusty volumes of history; but the Canada Pension Plan changes that we now have before us will still be affecting the lives of millions of Canadians.
I would venture to suggest to my hon. colleagues that there are few issues of greater concern to all Canadians than the evolution and sound financial management of a social insurance program which provides Canadian workers and their dependent family members with protection against the loss of employment income in the event of retirement, disability and death. Furthermore, I believe that the legislation to amend the Canada Pension Plan is the capstone to federal-provincial initiatives which will result in a wide range of benefit enrichments, as well as in the establishment of a financing arrangement to ensure the plan's long-term stability.
The Canada Pension Plan came into being 20 years ago in 1966 as a result of foresight and co-operation among federal and provincial legislators at the time. The plan's benefits and benefit levels were established in response to the economic needs and social attitudes of the day. It was agreed at the outset that any major changes to the plan in future years would require the consent of both the federal Parliament and two-thirds of the provinces having two-thirds of the Canadian population.

During the last two decades, the CPP has served Canadians well. With the federal Old Age Security program, it forms the solid basis for pension income for Canadian workers. As we know, many of these workers have yet to enjoy adequate
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
protection under an employer-sponsored plan, especially if they frequently change jobs-something which is becoming more and more necessary nowadays. And since CPP benefits are fully portable, the plan is the most important vehicle for providing income for retired workers.
I believe it is also appropriate to note that the federal Government, in addition to spearheading reforms to the Canada Pension Plan, has taken the lead in the area of reform of private employer-sponsored pension plans. While the majority of these plans fall under the direct jurisdiction of the provincial Governments, we have introduced legislation which will amend the federal Pension Benefits Standards Act which governs employer-sponsored pension plans in such federally regulated institutions as banks, railways, telecommunications services and federal Crown corporations.
The proposed amendments to the Pension Benefits Standards Act will implement important provisions for improved portability of pensions as well as earlier vesting of pension credits and greater flexibility in the age of eligibility for retirement benefits. I know that reform has been long sought by many people both in the House and out. These people have pointed out the need for vesting and portability in private pension plans and I am pleased to see that the Government and Parliament are moving very rapidly to fulfil those legislative requirements.
Moreover, we have consulted closely with the provincial Governments on the entire field of pension reform. Most of the provinces have indicated their intention to amend their own pension standards legislation and I am confident that in the wake of current federal and provincial initiatives, Canadians can look forward to a significantly great degree of uniformity in pension standards throughout the country in coming years. As Hon. Members know, standardization is important in a federal state such as Canada. In the past, it has been disquieting when people who wish for employment reasons to move from one province to another fear for their pension credits.
The continuation of federal-provincial initiatives such as those which have culminated in the reforms of the Canada Pension Plan encourages me, and, I am sure, all Hon. Members, to maintain a spirit of optimism for continued progress in the development of Canada's pension system. I must add that the co-operation of Canada's Parliamentarians from all sides toward reform of the nation's pension system has been a demonstration of the best aspects of democracy in action. I would like particularly to commend my two critics, the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) and the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), who not only have co-operated but have put forward suggestions. From time to time, people decry the way Parliamentarians act, but I think people will look back at the manner in which this matter has been handled and will feel that it was one of the brighter spots in Parliament with all sides acting together on behalf of Canadians.

June 11, 1986
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN AND THE FEDERAL COURT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN AND THE FEDERAL COURT
speechtext:
This non-partisan attitude has been evident through the consultation and discussion processes, particularly in the work of the special committee on pension reform, many of whose recommendations are addressed in the legislation that amends the Canada Pension Plan and the Pension Benefits Standards Act to which I have already referred.
Of course, the federal Government has also supported and implemented improvements in the income-tested benefits that are provided over and above the Old Age Security Program to low-income Canadians who have not had the opportunity to make adequate provision for retirement income. Even before we formed the new federal Government in September 1984, we supported the $50 monthly increase in the Guaranteed Income Supplement for needy single pensioners age 65 and over. This increase achieved two important objectives. It brought the income guarantee for single pensioners to a level that ensured a more decent minimum income for all of its recipients and it also implemented greater parity between single and married pensioners who qualified for the supplement. Nevertheless, during the 1984 election campaign, we indicated to Canadian voters that we were concerned about a significant anomaly in the income-tested spouse's allowance which provides benefits to eligible persons in the 60 to 64 age category who meet the residence requirements for the Old Age Security Program.
At the time, under the legislation, some widows and widowers could qualify for this benefit and others could not. A widowed person's eligibility for this allowance depended on the age of both partners in a marriage at the time one partner died. We promised that we would terminate this obvious inequity and introduce legislation to provide the spouse's allowance to all low-income widows and widowers in the 60 to 64 age group regardless of the age of their spouses at the time of death. This commitment was an immediate priority when we assumed office and, as Hon. Members present will recall, the necessary legislation received Royal Assent by the end of June 1985, and the new widowed spouse's allowance became payable the following September extending benefits to thousands of needy Canadians who had been denied them under previous legislation.
Of course, improvements in social programs must always be carefully considered by the Government in light of present and projected financial considerations. Indeed, because expenditures on social programs normally involve a continuing and escalating outlay, there is probably no area of spending that must be subject to more careful thought. This guiding principle applies equally to changes under a program such as the Old Age Security Program which is funded entirely from general taxation revenues and to a contributory program such as the Canada Pension Plan which is self-financing, being entirely funded by its members' contributions and the interest earned by the investment of surplus money in the plan's fund. In both cases, it is the money of workers and taxpayers that is
paying for benefits, and the Government believes that Canadians should demand top value for their dollars which they pay in taxes or contributions toward those programs.
In the case of the Canada Pension Plan, it is necessary to obtain a federal-provincial consensus on major changes. This is required not only because of the unique rules for provincial consent to Canada Pension Plan changes but also because of the need for parallelism between the federal plan and its counterpart in Quebec, the Quebec Pension Plan. Discussions involving my Department, the Department of Finance and the provincial Governments were put in high gear very soon after the 1984 election and led to the federal-provincial agreement announced in December of last year. The results of these discussions are put in concrete terms in the Bill before the House today.
I think it is also important to pay special attention to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who, with his provincial counterparts, negotiated many of the financial aspects of this Bill. It is important to note that when this legislation was passed by the House, in its wisdom, in 1966-and I think the House was right to do so, not only because I am Minister of National Health and Welfare-the House saw this as a social policy initiative rather than a finance initiative. It is important as well to show co-operation among the various finance Ministers, both federal and provincial, and I commend and thank them for that co-operation at this time.
Four concerns dominated the federal-provincial discussions: first, maintaining the long-term health of the plan's fund; second, ensuring the affordability of premiums paid by working Canadians and their employers; third, adapting benefits to the changing needs of Canadians; and fourth, maintaining parallelism between the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan.
To meet the objective of putting the plan on a sound and stable footing for the future in the fairest and least disruptive way, it is proposed that gradual increases in the annual contribution rate will take effect each year beginning January 1, 1987. These rate increases will follow a 25-year schedule. Rates will increase by 0.2 per cent per year for the first five years of the schedule and by 0.15 per cent for the remaining 20 years. Therefore, by the year 2011-and obviously I invite all Hon. Members to be here at that time-the contribution rate will stand at 7.6 per cent, and of course workers and employers will each continue to pay half of the total contributions.
For Canadians earning an average wage, the premium increase in the first year of the new rates will add approximately $26 to the amount which they will contribute annually. In addition to the increase which will result from the annual growth in the year's maximum pensionable earnings for Canada Pension Plan purposes, or the YMPE as my colleagues will come to know it during this debate, it should be noted that the impact of the increases on take-home pay will always be
June 11, 1986

less than actual contribution increases because plan contributions are deductible for income tax purposes.
Two additional measures are proposed to ensure the stability of the Canada Pension Plan. The size of the plan's fund will be targeted to be approximately equal to two years of benefits in the long term rather than the present six years. This will guarantee a reserve sufficiently large to cushion the effects of economic and demographic fluctuations without building up a needlessly large and costly fund. By the year 2011, the fund will be slightly above the target in order to provide the cushion needed prior to the retirement of the so-called baby boom generation.
It is important for Canadians to know-and I think Hon. Members have been asked these questions in their ridings- whether the fund is solvent and whether there will something left when they retire. I want to tell them today that the fund is solvent, is in good hands, is paying its own way, and is secure. Yes, Canadians are contributing to the Canada Pension Plan fund which will pay them the benefits we are describing today.
There will be a procedure to review the financing of the plan at five-year intervals in the future, thereby ensuring that Canada Pension Plan finances are in good shape, that the contribution rate increase schedule is on track, and that there is always a 20-year to 25-year schedule of rates in place in advance.
As I indicated at the outset of my comments today, we have also secured agreement on a package of important Canada Pension Plan benefit reforms which nevertheless will have only a moderate impact upon long-term costs of the plan. Perhaps the most important feature of this reform package, the feature which will benefit the largest portion of plan contributors as soon as it is implemented, is the provision for greater flexibility in the age of eligibility for retirement benefits under the plan.
Before getting into the details of the changes, perhaps I should tell the House what we as a federal Government thought was most important. Not only did we want to guarantee the viability of the plan and to assure Canadians of its financial stability, we were absolutely insistent in the negotiations that we use the opportunity, whereby we knew we had to increase the contribution rate to improve the plan at the same time. The plan in 1966 was a good one, and it is a good one today. However, we knew there could be improvements. I know my hon. colleagues in the Opposition will say that there could be additional improvements to the plan, and I agree with that as well. What I am saying is that we should use every opportunity we have, as we have now done because the plan had to be reviewed from the point of view of its financial viability, to bring in improvements to a pension plan for which Canadians had paid.
As I have already mentioned, the benefit in the plan which I think will receive the most attention is the matter of flexible retirement entry. I should point out to Hon. Members that this provision is already in place in the Quebec Pension Plan. When I speak about parallelism, the Quebec Pension Plan in a
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
number of ways, especially in this provision, has shown leadership in terms of bringing in new adjustments to reflect more closely the situation in the workplace and the retirement requirements of Canadians. I am pleased that the Canada Pension Plan is reflecting what has already taken place in Quebec.
To date, plan contributors cannot begin to receive their retirement benefits until the month following their sixty-fifth birthday. There has always been a provision whereby persons who wish to continue working and contributing to the plan beyond this age could do so until age 70. However, this provision was usually beneficial only to individuals with very short contributory histories. Essentially the plan gave them no compensation for the years of benefit payments they were giving up by delaying receipt of their pension.
Under the new provision, all contributors to the Canada Pension Plan will be able to co-ordinate the plan with their personal retirement arrangements. Contributors will be able to make a choice to begin receiving their Canada Pension Plan retirement benefits at the most appropriate time from the age of 60 through to the age of 70 with corresponding actuarial adjustments. The way in which the provision will work is that when a contributor chooses to begin receiving his or her retirement benefits sooner than age 65 and after age 60, the pension will be calculated in a normal way according to the contributor's earning history. Then it will be reduced by one-half of one per cent for each month prior to the month following his or her sixty-fifth birthday. This means that there will be a reduction rate of 6 per cent per year and a maximum reduction of 30 per cent if the contributor begins receiving the pension at age 60. Similarly, the pension will be increased by as much as 30 per cent for a contributor who delays the start of benefits until age 70. As well, contributors will have to meet a test of full or partial cessation of employment in order to qualify for the Canada Pension Plan benefits prior to age 65.
Given this range of potential reductions and increases, individual contributors' choices as to when to begin receiving benefits will be very important and should not be taken lightly. However, the Government feels that Canadians have both the right and the responsibility to make these choices for themselves, and that Governments should do what they can to help them tailor their retirement income plans to their individual needs.
I should like to put it in very human terms. I refer to a cartoon which I saw in one of the national newspapers last weekend. It showed a gentleman reading a newspaper which indicated that he could now retire at age 60, and its caption was "Free at last". Perhaps that describes the attitude of some Canadians to this provision better than I can describe it.
The new provision will be especially advantageous to individuals who find themselves out of work in their early sixties and are confronted with limited job prospects for unemployed individuals in that age category. The provision will also help workers whose private employer-sponsored pension plans offer options for early retirement. In such cases,

June 11, 1986
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
the company pension alone is not always sufficient to meet the income requirements, and he or she therefore is unable to take advantage of the option. Under the new legislation, however, workers who have this option will also be able to receive an early retirement pension from the Canada Pension Plan. In combination with the company pension, this should make it easier for them to retire sooner than age 65 if they truly wish to do so. We estimate that there are about 175,000 contributors in their early sixties who will want to take immediate advantage of this provision, or at least to look at the provision to see whether or not they want to follow those options. Moreover, I would like to emphasize that the implementation of this provision for flexible retirement will not add to the long term costs of the plan.
Another major benefit improvement, Mr. Speaker, one of which I am especially proud, will be a substantial increase in disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan so that the maximum monthly disability benefit in 1987 should be in excess of $600, a dramatic increase over the 1986 maximum of $455. Moreover, because this increase is being applied to the fiat rate portion of the benefit rather than to the variable, earnings related portion, there are about 155,000 current CPP disability pensioners who will see a significant rise in their payments next year.
As well, Mr. Speaker, the contributory rules for the plan's disability benefits will be relaxed, allowing workers who become disabled to qualify for benefits if they have contributed to the plan during two of the three years preceding their disablement; and the requirement that applicants must have contributed for at least one-third of their contributory period will be removed. As a result of these changes, an additional 5,000 people could qualify for benefits next year.
Under the Government's new legislation there will also be significant improvements in combined benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. The ceiling on combined disability and survival benefits, for example, will be increased to accommodate the higher fiat rate benefit. The maximum combined pension in 1987 will be in excess of $700 per month. This change, Mr. Speaker, will also benefit as many as 5,000 people.
The ceiling on combined retirement and survivor benefits after age 65 will remain at the level of the maximum retirement pension during the year in which the combined benefit becomes payable. However, there will be simplifications in the calculation of such a combined benefit and this will result in increased payments to about 25,000 people during the first year of implementation.
There will also be a new category of combined pensions where a survivor beneficiary under age 65 has chosen to receive a flexible retirement benefit. New rules to cover this category of combined pensions are laid out in the Bill as well.
An important further provision regarding survivor benefits under the plan is that, starting next year, such benefits will no longer be withdrawn from a widow or widower upon remarriage. Benefits will be restored, on application, to former recipients whose benefits had been previously withdrawn upon remarriage. We estimate that some 35,000 people will qualify for reinstatment of their Canada Pension Plan survivor benefits as a result of this provision.
In preparing this package of benefit enrichments, the federal and provincial government representatives have been concerned with the need for improvement in the various forms of pension coverage that are available to women. Traditionally, women in Canada have experienced a greater degree of financial hardship during their senior years than men, and I am especially pleased that several features in the Government's legislation to modify the Canada Pension Plan particularly addressed the needs of women in retirement.
The improvements in survivor benefits, which I have just mentioned, are one part of these provisions. Another is the amendment which will ensure that, upon divorce, Canada Pension Plan pension credits earned by both partners in a marriage will be subject to sharing between the former spouses, without application, as soon as the necessary information is received by the planned administration. Similarly, when married couples separate or when common-law couples part, the division of the pension credits earned during the marriage or relationship will be mandatory upon application by one spouse. As well, Canada Pension Plan pensions earned during a marriage will be shared equally between spouses upon retirement if one of the spouses so requests. For this provision to apply, both spouses will have to be at least 60 years old and have ceased contributing to the plan. Spouses will have the right to preclude a division of pension credits or sharing of pensions, but only by mutual agreement explicitly referring to their Canada Pension Plan rights.
And finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to a small but important change governing the provision of children's benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. At present, the Plan pays a $91 monthly benefit in respect of a child of a contributor if the contributor dies or becomes disabled. We are now proposing to double the benefit in the cases in which the employment income of both parents is lost as a result of death or disability.
There are other provisions, but I do not have the time today, nor do I want to take up even more time of the House than I have already, relating to adoption. I have been concerned about what I think are archaic rules regarding the rights of adopted children. In some cases in federal legislation the rights of adopted children are not equal to those of children born to a family where benefits of the various provisions flow naturally and normally to a child. I would think the benefits in federal legislation generally-I am giving it as a general principle- should apply equally to adopted children as to those born to a family. I will not go into those details but I think in that area the same conditions will now apply under the Canada Pension
June 11, 1986

Plan for adopted children as for other children. That is a step forward, Mr. Speaker.
As I indicated earlier, these reforms to benefits and funding under the Canada Pension Plan have come about as the result of exceptional communication and co-operation among governments. The federal-provincial discussions which have culminated in the legislation now before Parliament have demonstrated that when responsible, committed Canadians agree on a mutual objective, they are able to arrive at a consensus which reaches across the borders between different levels of governments and Parties. Today, therefore, I wish to offer my most sincere expression of personal gratitude for the spirit of co-operation which has been evident from Hon. Members from all Parties in examining this legislation. I am not hopeful that Parliament, in giving this legislation its final consideration and in exercising further this co-operative spirit, will pass it with the expedience it obviously deserves and that the Bill will receive Royal Assent before the summer recess.
I am making this request to my hon. colleagues, because three major steps remain to consolidate these reforms to the Canada Pension Plan. First, the provincial Governments, which indicated their provisional agreement on the proposed legislation last December, must conclude their own ratification procedures before the end of this year. Second, my department must prepare for the implementation of substantial changes in the Plan's administration. Just as an aside, we have 19.5 million Canadians on record and every time a person contributes to the Plan, every Canadian employed, self-employed or otherwise, those changes have to occur and have to be accurate for each individual. It is the people's fund and their plan. I think Members of the House will see very quickly why the lead-up period of at least six months for implementing such changes for January 1, 1987 is needed to affect this in an administrative sense. Third, my officials must also prepare and disseminate important information about coming improvements in the Canada Pension Plan, both for current contributors to the Plan and for current and future beneficiaries. I call on Hon. Members of the House to use either their householder mailings, their good offices or contact with their constituents to indicate the changes coming about. They are complex and it is important that Canadians understand and know them.
In terms of disability, I am looking at getting a communication to doctors across the country. They might have information available, and as a person applies possibly for disability, the doctors will know the time frame in which the application has to be made. In that way people will not lose the benefits to which they may be entitled because of lack of knowledge of the regulations and provisions. There is obviously still a lot of work to be done on this matter.
I know that all of my colleagues in Cabinet, especially the Minister of Finance with whom I have shared jurisdiction over the preparation of this landmark legislation, join me in emphasizing the importance of ensuring its prompt passage so
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
that we can provide much needed and much anticipated improvements in Canada Pension Plan benefits to Canadians in January of next year.

Mr. Speaker, we are well aware that even after these chages to the Canada Pension Plan have been implemented, there will always be room for improvement in this area, and I am referring both to the Canada Pension Plan and to the other public and private programs that make up of the retirement income apparatus in this country.

During discussions on the provision of improved retirement income for homemakers, including proposals to incorporate such a provision into the Canada Pension Plan as Members would also like us to proceed with, we will examine and seek solutions to the complex questions of equity, cost, and other related issues so that the necessary steps can be taken to achieve solid improvements in this area.
As I am sure my hon. colleagues can appreciate, this is a subject with broad social and economic implications. Nonetheless, the federal Government recognizes the importance for all Canadians of work done in the home. We want to ensure that homemakers can look forward to their retirement years without fear for their financial security. I am especially pleased that the provinces have agreed to pursue this subject further.
I am convinced that that is the next frontier in pension reform. I personally believe that the best vehicle is the Canada Pension Plan. There may be some who believe that there should be another vehicle, a separate account. I would like to have that discussed. I do know that just as we give value to and can administer work which is related to earnings, the time for a homemakers pension has come for work related to the home which builds the mortar and bricks on which the family unit is based. A homemakers pension is valid and Parliament should take upon itself responsibility to ensure that this next step is taken before long.
In closing, I believe that the Canada Pension Plan reform legislation now before us and the commitment of federal and provincial Governments to pursue further improvements in the area of pension reform are a salutory affirmation of the parliamentary process as it continues to serve Canada with distinction.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to preface my remarks this afternoon by thanking the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for the compliments which he gave me and the Member for Beaches (Mr. Young). It is precedent setting in the sense that all three Parties in the House have allowed this legislation to proceed in order that we can pass this Bill before the end of June. I would like to thank the chairman of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare, the Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) for the work which he did as well.

Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN AND THE FEDERAL COURT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN AND THE FEDERAL COURT
speechtext:
Due to the precedent-setting way in which we have introduced this Bill, Members of the Opposition will not be allowed to introduce amendments to the legislation at committee stage. For that reason, in the latter part of my remarks I will put clearly on record the way in which the Liberal Party would have moved to improve the legislation had we had the opportunity to do so.
I first commenced to gain knowledge of the subject matter when I was asked by the previous Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Hon. Monique Begin, to head a task force in the early winter of 1983 to study two particular areas. The first was private pension plan legislation in the country and the second was public pension plan systems in the country. We were very fortunate that during the 10 months in which we studied that subject matter all three political Parties approached the matter on the basis of arriving at a consensus to allow us to move forward with the legislation program on the much needed reforms to both private and public pension plans.
It is a compliment to the parliamentary system that we were able to produce a largely consensual document in December of 1983. For that reason alone we are today advancing to the legislative agenda the much needed pension reform in the country. While we are paying compliments, we should compliment the members of that committee from three years ago because they were instrumental in allowing us to come to grips with the legislative agenda on pension reform.
During those 10 months of study in 1983 I learned that the subject matter is very complex. The more I thought I knew about the subject matter, the more I learned that I did not know about it. That having been said, as always happens, there came a day when the political parties had to make decisions on the improvement of pension legislation. We did so in December of 1983.
There were two major reasons why we required pension reform in the country. The first was the new emerging work patterns in the country which were totally different than the work patterns of my father's generation. The second reason is the monumental changes in lifestyle. With regard to lifestyle, I speak of the regrettable fact that we have a much higher rate of marriage breakdown in the country today than we had in previous generations. For that reason, many of the recommendations of the task force which you will see in Bill C-116 and Bill C-90, the Act relating to the private pension area, are much needed.
With regard to emerging work patterns, people who go into the workforce can be expected to work in two or three different provinces during their lifetime. They can be expected to be retrained at certain points during their work career. As a result, the system must become much more flexible and affordable. Many of the recommendations in this legislation and Bill C-90 were made as a result of those two emerging patterns.
I would like to indicate to the House why the Liberal Party decided to allow swift passage of this legislation. However, since we are not allowed to move amendments, I think it is necessary to put on the public record the amendments we would have moved to the legislation.
The agreement was reached because, frankly, the legislation before us is better than the legislation which presently exists. It goes a long way to addressing the needs of my own constituents and other working Canadians. I recognize that if we were not able to pass this legislation by the end of June the improvements to public pension legislation would have been delayed by a year. Rather than being able to institute these changes by January 1, 1987, they would have been delayed until January of 1988.
Having become intimately involved with the subject matter, I can appreciate the problem of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Once one has mastered the subject matter, it is still difficult to transverse the regulatory mechanism in order to attain the changes. The Minister stated previously that it requires the agreement of two-thirds of the population representing two-thirds of the provinces in order to accommodate change to the public pension plan system. Therefore, even though you have finally reached the position, it takes a lot longer to arrive at a consensus among the provincial Governments. I recognize that is a major obstacle, hence an added reason for realizing that the Minister has already negotiated to the best of his ability a consensus package with his provincial counterparts. I will be the last one to stand in the way because I also recognize the complexity of that kind of negotiation.
I happen to believe, as the Minister does, and I think as the Hon. Member for Beaches does, that this is a very unique way of introducing legislative change on the floor of the House of Commons. Hopefully it can become a model, to some extent. We talk about the need for parliamentary reform, and that is a prime area where individual Members of Parliament can have some influence on the way in which legislative programs come into being. 1 hope that in future, prior to the Government entering negotiations with the provinces in order to attain this kind of change, it would feel able to reference the changes to the standing committee so it can have some input to the agenda for negotiation with the provinces. I think that would be an added step towards meaningful parliamentary reform.
I would now like to focus on three key areas where I feel the Bill could have been approved. I speak now as the Member of Parliament for Sudbury. I hope the things I have to say will reflect many of the problems individual Members of Parliament have with their constituents.
In my own constituency the one area I have a great deal of difficulty with is that of CPP disability pensions. The majority of my constituency workload is in this area. I was hopeful that, having undertaken legislative reform of the CPP after 20 years, we would have been able to improve the Section dealing
June 11, 1986

with disability better than we have in this Bill today. The Minister has correctly stated that this Bill will significantly enhance disability benefits. It will increase the amount paid from $458 a month this year to a little over $600 a month next year. To me that was reason enough not to stand in the way of passage of this legislation.
However, once that is accomplished, the flat benefit portion of a CPP disability pension will still represent only 80 per cent of the Old Age Security cheque. I think all of us recognize that those 65 and over are relatively well protected by the social safety net in place. Where we have problems is in the age bracket of 45 to 64. If a Canadian falls victim to a stroke or a heart attack, or has some long-term disability hit his family, and he has no private pension that will cover it, he falls solely into the arms of the Government for support. That is where our legislation is woefully inadequate. Even with this significant improvement, we still fall short of what is required for a decent standard of living.
This is where the Liberal Party differs. We would have preferred to have increased the fiat rate to 100 per cent of the OAS. In addition, on the earnings related portion, which will remain at, I believe, 75 per cent of the earnings component, we would have put forward as an objective 100 per cent replacement. We could therefore have significantly improved the standard of living of those individuals who have to rely solely on the disability benefits under the CPP. How much would that have cost contributors? Not very much. The package we are putting forward today is very modest, although a significant improvement. The cost of increasing the payments to the levels I suggest would not have cost more than a 0.2 per cent increase in the amount of contributions. I do not think there is a working Canadian who would object to an increased payment of $24 a year to obtain a better standard of living for those unfortunate enough to have to rely on a disability pension for their livelihood.
Most Members of Parliament recognize that our constituents must almost have one foot in the grave before they qualify for a CPP disability pension. Yet if there is one province which deserves credit for improving the legislation, that has to be the Province of Quebec. What we have seen tabled in this Bill today has been in effect in Quebec for the last four years. As well, in January, 1984 the Quebec Government changed the definition of disability for contributors between the ages of 60 and 64 to the following. They are considered disabled if they are incapable of carrying on a job they had before becoming disabled. That kind of change would have been an improvement of this legislation. The problem at present is that when people apply for a CPP disability pension, a civil servant can ask that person to seek employment in an area with which he is not familiar. That is in effect another way in which we block access to a disability pension. Therefore I would have preferred changes in the definition of disability to allow more Canadians the opportunity to obtain a disability pension.
Last but not least, I believe there should be changes made to the eligibility criteria with respect to the number of years
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
worked prior to the application. How many times has the bureaucracy, and this is not their fault because they are simply following regulations, refused a pension on the basis that the person should have applied for it prior to coming to us as Members of Parliament? There is absolutely nothing we can do once they come to us if they do not meet this particular eligibility requirement.
Having said all that, I want it clearly on the record that, despite these changes to the CPP, Parliament has to push forward on a national disability insurance plan. That is the only way in which I believe the public can best be served. It has to be separated from the CPP if we are going to properly address the needs of disabled Canadians. I just want it clearly on the record that in addition to those improvements in the Bill, the Liberal Party is in favour of the introduction of a national disability insurance scheme.
Another significant step forward, I believe, is the introduction of the concept of early retirement in this legislation. That is a very progressive step. It will allow someone the opportunity to take a pension as early as age 60, at a reduced amount. If at age 65 you are eligible for a $400 a month pension, and you take it at age 60, it will be reduced to $280. If you wait until age 70, it will be enhanced and could be worth as much as $700 a month. I hope our constituents understand that while this introduces the concept of flexible retirement, there will be a difference in the amount of pension that they can collect. Earlier flexible retirement is an excellent part of the legislation.
There is one area that I believe Parliament should consider when it next undertakes reform. It is the way in which the Canada Pension Plan is stacked and integrated with private pension plans. While Parliament is going to significantly improve early retirement benefits and disability benefits, I find it objectionable that we have not dealt with the workers who have access to a private pension plan at their place of employment. For every extra dollar we give today, they will lose a dollar from their private pension. I think that is a sad reflection on the way we, as legislators, have failed to protect workers' interests in this country. We could have also made significant improvements if we had studied this particular area.
I have already talked about how emerging lifestyles impacted on the legislation before us. As well, I stated that some 40 per cent of today's marriages break down. Significant portions of this legislation and Bill C-90 will go a long way to improving the lot of women in our society, because this is largely a woman's issue.
The Minister already noted the effects of survivors' benefits. The measures in the legislation which dispel the idea that one is no longer chattel in this country are a significant improvement. Previously, those who remarried lost survivors' benefits. Not only will that be corrected, it will be retroactive so that

June 11, 1986
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
people who previously lost benefits under survivors' benefits can apply to have them reinstated on January 1, 1987.
Last, but not least, I want to talk about the inclusion of home-makers in the Canada Pension Plan. I recognize, as does the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that there is significant public opinion on our side in allowing the introduction of home-makers into the Canada Pension Plan. This has only been a result of changes in provincial Governments in the Province of Quebec and the Province in Ontario. Those provinces, because of their size, effectively had a veto. Now that those provinces are at least in favour of the principle of the inclusion of home-makers in the public pension plan area, I think we have a reasonable opportunity to reddress a wrong that was done with the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan in 1966. I believe that when we allowed the workers of that generation to have access to a public pension plan in 1966, we should have embarked upon a study of the concept of a home-maker at that time.
The Canada Pension Plan was phased in over ten years after its introduction in 1966. Public pension plans operate in a way totally different from the private pension and people should understand that the public pension system is probably the best bargain for any worker in this and the previous generation. In the previous generation, for every dollar of benefit derived from the Canada Pension Plan, those contributors paid only 17 cents. The other 83 cents has been transferred to the next generation of Canadians, who include the Pages in the House. They will be paying the other 83 cents.
When we studied whether or not we should expand the Canada Pension Plan, we made sure that the recommendations we made to Parliament would not place an undue burden on the next generation. I have no fear about the solvency of the Canada Pension Plan, but it should be made clear that the Canada Pension Plan will remain solvent so long as that burden that we transfer to the next generation of Canadians can be tolerated. The moment we go beyond that, we are in danger of reneging on the intergenerational transfer of responsibility from one generation to the other. That fact bears close scrutiny when we undertake any future changes to the Canada Pension Plan.
During the ten-year phase-in of this plan from 1966, we were dealing with a male versus female problem. In those days, the majority of the workforce was male. Parliament was allowing them the best opportunity at the best bargain price to enter into a public pension plan, but we did not allow the mothers of that generation the same opportunity. They had worked equally hard to build the infrastructure in this country that my generation and future generations would be allowed to enjoy. That is why I am greatly in favour of the inclusion of homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan and I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will strongly recommend homemakers to be included retroactively. The cost involved in giving our parents' generation an equal opportunity is not great. We are talking about those born since in 1901. I
hope the Minister strongly urges retroactivity with respect to homemakers.
In the event that we are unable to successfully negotiate the inclusion of homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan, I want the public record to show that the Liberal Party will consider the Cofirentes model with respect to an improvement in the Canada Pension Plan.
Let me explain the Cofirentes model. The present Canada Pension Plan only replaces 25 per cent of the average industrial wage for those Canadian workers who earn one-half or less of the average industrial wage. The Cofirentes model, recognizing the need for low-income workers to have more of their pension requirements met by the public pension system, recommends an increase from 25 per cent to 50 per cent for the first half of the average industrial wage, while maintaining the Canada pension replacement at 25 per cent for the next half of the average industrial wage. In the event that homemakers are not included in the public pension plan system, I am stating for the record that we should be considering an option like the Cofirentes model for improving the lot of lower income working Canadians.

I support this measure and I hope we will have an opportunity to hear and question witnesses in committee. I am sure of that. I can appreciate the problem of the Minister and Parliament.
If we want to change the law we must have the co-operation of all Parties in the House. Today, Mr. Speaker, I am proud to give my support and to co-operate because, after studying this problem for a number of years, I am sure that the measure introduced today will improve the situation of Canadian workers.

Having said that, I know that the Hon. Member for Beaches wishes to join in the debate. subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN AND THE FEDERAL COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, let me say that the co-operation that has been shown by members in my Party will continue in order to ensure the speedy passage of this Bill prior to the House rising for the summer recess. Let me also say that I have enjoyed working with the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) and the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), who was the Chairman of our
June 11, 1986

committee, as we tried to work through what I have previously described as a rather difficult but unique process. It has been difficult because of the nature of negotiations between the federal and provincial Governments with respect to bringing amendments to the Canada Pension Plan forward. While I appreciate that, and support the amendments in so far as they go-I believe they are a vast improvement over what presently exists-it does not mean I am entirely happy with the process or the question of whether the amendments go far enough or even whether the amendments will do what we like to believe they will do, and I will come back to that momentarily.
As has been pointed out, the amendments cover such things as early retirement, improvement in disability benefits, improvements in the area of credit and pension splitting and survivor benefits. We have gone through this lengthy and difficult process of negotiation with the provinces and the federal Government to arrive at the amendments now before us, and what disturbs me is that this is the first time in 20 years that there has been a major review of this plan.
I suggested to the Minister in committee the other evening that it is not satisfactory for an agreement to be negotiated, arrived at and concluded, then simply brought back to the House of Commons for our stamp of approval, because we cannot offer any amendments to the proposals which are before us. I suggested to the Minister, and I would suggest to any other Minister who is involved in much of the same kind of process, that some mechanism must be found where the Opposition Parties in the House of Commons are consulted in a very real way about the manner in which the negotiations between the federal and provincial Governments are carried out. I say to you in all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, that both the Hon. Member for Sudbury and myself, on behalf of my Party, could have been quite helpful in that process.
I understand there are still some negotiations to be carried out with the Province of Ontario. I am hopeful that at least on an experimental basis some all Party discussions can take place on a unified Canadian position with that province or with any other province in future negotiation. I think it would be a good thing to do. Not only would it be a good thing to do in terms of what we are interested in, but certainly in the spirit of Parliamentary reform. So I strongly recommend that to the Minister. Knowing him from the years I have worked with him, I am sure he will be open to that suggestion. Perhaps he will take it up with his officials to see if some mechanism can be worked out to accommodate that need.
As the Minister said in his opening remarks, he would be quite surprised if Members of the Opposition did not offer some criticism. I do not want to surprise him. I am sure he expects us to say a few words, albeit, not harsh words, about the Bill before us.
First, I really think we have missed an opportunity to take a hard look at how we could improve the benefit pay-out to all contributors to the Canada Pension Plan. There have been a
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
number of recommendations made by various Parties over the years who have recognized that the Canada Penson Plan is probably, next to the Old Age Security Act, the best way of providing an adequate income when people retire. My colleague who is no longer with us, but who certainly served on the committee which took a look at parliamentary reform, Ted Miller, argued very strongly that there should be an increase in pension benefit pay-out to equal about 50 per cent of the average industrial wage. As we know, at least half of the people who are employed in Canada are not covered by private pension plans. For many of those Canadians it means looking forward to the so-called golden age of retirement as the golden age of poverty. It is a fact that 6 elderly single women out of 10 over the age of 65 are living on incomes well below the poverty line. In a country as rich as Canada, with our resources, potential and people, I think that is a national disgrace. In a country as rich as Canada, the fact that we allow 6 elderly single women out of every 10 over the age of 65 to live in poverty is not acceptable today, if it was ever acceptable before. It is something we should be able to do something about.
While I am on that subject, there is also a large population of single elderly women who have never had an opportunity to participate in the Canada Pension Plan and, therefore, are not elegible for a benefit under the CPP. There is a real need to do something about that group of Canadians. Unfortunately, the way the CPP is structured at the present time there is no relief. Certainly I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare is taking a look at the Old Age Security Program to increase benefits in order to give some relief to that large group of single elderly women.
I would like to pose the question, Mr. Speaker, why the Government felt it necessary, when it loosened up the retirement age from 65 years to 60, to make the formula for reduction in pension benefits in the area of 6 per cent per year of early retirement? That will not be much of an inducement to take early retirement. If the object of the exercise is not only to improve pension benefits for Canada's elderly, but also to allow younger people to enter the workforce, I do not think a 30 per cent reduction in pension, if a person elects to retire at age 60, is much of an encouragement for that individual to leave the workforce. Many people cannot afford to live on that kind of income. I would have much preferred a formula more in line with what has been accepted in many private plans, which is something like a 4 per cent reduction in each year of early retirement rather than the 6 per cent proposed by the Government.
With respect to disbility benefits, I would agree with the Hon. Member for Sudbury. I had the opportunity of working on another committee with the Hon. Member for Oxford. It was a Special Committee on the Disabled and Handicapped in the last Parliament. Fortunately, that committee has now been struck as a permanent subcommittee which I hope will go on beyond this session, because it is of such value to the disabled community. However, in the previous committee we presented

June 11, 1986
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
a report to the Elouse of Commons which was entitled "The Obstacles Report". Recommendations Nos. 39 and 40 in the report of that committee, which was an all Party committee, strongly recommended the setting up of a national disability insurance program for very good reasons, and I will not go into all of them today. We recognize that there are a large number of Canadians who have never been in the workforce and who will probably never enter it simply because they are disabled or handicapped to such an extent that they cannot perform within the workforce as we understand it. For them there is no such thing as a disability benefit under the Canada Pension Plan. We felt that a more sensible approach would be to set up a national disability insurance program to take into account that approximate 10 per cent of the population which is excluded. Not all of them are excluded at the present time, but certainly a great many of them are. For example, within the visually impaired community in Canada the unemployment rate is in excess of 90 per cent. In other words, if one happens to be visually impaired, or what is called legally blind, one's chances of finding employment in the regular workforce are practically zilch. It seems to us that a much better way of dealing with this problem would be to set up a national disability insurance program.
Every Member of the House who has ever dealt with a constituent who has attempted to obtain a disability benefit under the Canada Pension plan is as familiar with the problems as I am. First, in order to receive a disability benefit under the CPP one has to be practically comatose or bedridden. That is much too difficult a requirement to meet to make one eligible for a disability pension. While we applaud the increase in disability benefits proposed by the Minister, and while we very much agree with the proposed amendment which would allow a person who has been in the workforce for two years out of the last three to become eligible for disability benefits, I suggest that in many cases it is not helpful to a great many people unless they become eligible for the program in some other way. I would like to see a loosening up of that eligibility requirement. I agree that it is probably too late in dealing with these amendments to do much about that. But certainly in the next round of negotiations between the federal Government and the provinces the whole question of disability benefit eligibility requirements should be high on the list of priorities for negotiation.
I welcome the Minister's remarks today in which he said that his Department would step up a national program to the medical profession with respect to disability requirements setting out what is required of individuals in terms of contribution records in order at least to qualify to apply for a benefit. I say to the Minister quite plainly that if his Department wishes to put together some type of explanatory package which is easily handled and easily read I would certainly be interested in including such a package in the reports I mail out to my constituents. I would recommend to members of my caucus
and to other Members of Parliament that they take advantage of this type of offer if it is forthcoming.
If there is one major problem that people have out there it is with respect to the lack of information on a whole host of government programs. It is also difficult to disseminate this information. However, if the medical profession were made aware of what is available to their patients, that would go a long way toward solving many of the problems we now have about how people find out what is available to them in terms of disability benefits. I welcome any offer that comes from the Minister's Department in that respect.
There is another area with which I wish to deal. I see that Section 116(2) of the existing legislation has had some minor amendments to it. As I understand the section, whenever any amendments are introduced or presented to the House the Chief Actuary is supposed to provide us with cost and impact figures with respect to what we are proposing to do under the Canada Pension Plan. I have not received those figures. I do not know whether the Chief Actuary has actually done that or not. However, he is supposed to do it with due haste and speed. The quicker I get my hands on that material, the better off I will be. It will provide some insight with respect to just what the costing is. Perhaps it will even erase some of the concerns I have at the present time. If such information is available I would like to receive it before we get into report stage and third reading of this Bill.
I would now like to deal with two other areas, one of which the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) touched upon in his speech. I also spoke about it at great length when Bill C-90 was before the House. When someone leaves his employment due to a disability, at the present time under most private plans there is a benefit that is generally described as a bridging benefit. In other words, the individual receives a pension earned up to the point of leaving employment. There is usually then a supplemental benefit paid which equals either Old Age Security benefits, which would otherwise be received at the age of 65, or, in some cases, the full equivalent of Canada Pension Plan benefits, which would otherwise be received at the age of 65. However, what happens is that if this individual applies for a disability benefit under the Canada Pension Plan, usually on the advice of a physician, and the eligiblity is determined and accepted and the individual actually receives a disability benefit, then the insurance company immediately deducts dollar-for-dollar off the amount that it paid to this individual. I am fearful that unless something is done under this legislation to prohibit such a practice, then all we are doing as a result of increasing the disability allowance is in effect giving the private insurance companies a windfall. It will be those companies which benefit and not the recipient of the disability benefit under the Canada Pension Plan.
There are other areas which I am not sure the Government has considered. Under some plans in which an individual is entitled, as a bridging benefit, to full CPP benefits as if he had worked until the age of 65, if that individual decides to retire at age 60 on January 1 of a given year with a 6 per cent
June 11, 1986

reduction for each year of early retirement, does this mean that the employer will then turn around and say: "Look, the legislation does not say you should receive 100 per cent Canada Pension Plan so therefore we will reduce our pension pay-out to you by 30 per cent"? I do not know whether or not the Government considered the matter when it was discussing these amendments. If it has not, then it would be very useful if it did something with the regulations that would prohibit the private insurance companies from receiving a windfall profit, as I have suggested.
While the Government's proposed splitting of pension credits on marriage breakdown has gone as far as it should probably go, I am a bit disappointed by the proposals for the splitting of pension benefits at age 65 between married couples or at age 60 if the couples have elected early retirement. I am disappointed because that is elective rather than mandatory. One or the other spouse would have to elect to split that pension benefit rather than have it be mandatory.
As long as I have been around here, women's organizations and others concerned about pension matters have argued loud, clear and long on that matter for very good reason. For example, in the case of a marriage breakdown, there are an awful lot of sharp lawyers out there with sharp pencils who attempt to make the pension credit a part of the divorce settlement by offering the woman a lump sum payment rather than the credit. Very often, because of the circumstances of the marriage breakdown, that lump sum seems to be attractive at that particular point in time. However, when the woman reaches age 65 and discovers how much pension she is about to receive, she then questions if it was indeed wise to accept the lump sum payments. Therefore, I would much prefer to have the proposal regarding pension splitting on retirement mandatory rather than elective.

Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
