Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to a question which I see as extremely important. However, I warm you that unlike the three previous speakers, my reaction to the Bill will be as negative as theirs was positive, if not more so. I shall explain.
If we look at the amendments proposed by the Minister, following consultations with the provinces, if we look at the figures released by the National Welfare Council in 1985 on the poverty profile, when we see that in 1984, 54 per cent of the elderly were living below the poverty line, and if you then ask me whether this Bill, together with Bill C-90, will remedy the situation, I have to say it will not.
Mr. Speaker, earlier we were looking at certain advantages of this Bill that would enable people to retire early and receive benefits under the Canada Pension Plan at age 60, as is already the case in Quebec, but subject to a penalty.
Mr. Speaker, when I see Members of this House, whatever their political stripe, who believe that this Bill will make it attractive for people to retire early, I think they are being very naive, because, this is another measure aimed at helping the rich. The benefits received under the Canada or the Quebec Pension Plan alone are not enough for a person to live on. It

June 11, 1986
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
means that this person has to have a good RRSP and a good private pension plan, to afford to draw his Canada Pension Plan benefits at a 5 per cent discount per year.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about early retirement and look at the whole range of important decisions that are supposed to make it attractive for people to take early retirement, I don't think that cutting unemployment insurance benefits for people who agree to retire early from a full-time job and find parttime work will do it, nor imposing a 5 per cent reduction in Quebec or Canada Pension Plan benefits as a condition for allowing people on average and low incomes to retire early and thus give younger people a chance.
Mr. Speaker, what the Canada Pension Plan Bill does is increase taxes. It will increase our taxes by $286 million in 1987, $615 million in 1988, $1.04 billion in 1989, and if no changes have been made by the year 2000, by $7,746 billion annually.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, there are provincial governments that owe considerable sums of money to the Canada Pension Plan, nearly $30 billion. The Province of Ontario alone owes $15 billion. These provinces are not being pressed to pay back what they owe. If they were, perhaps this would keep contribution levels from increasing so quickly or, if we were to increase contributions at the rate proposed in the Bill, we could then increase benefits by 50 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at this Bill and Bill C-90, which introduces changes to private pension plans, we see that both Bills are aimed at improving the situation and indeed, there is an improvement, but it benefits those who are well-off. Bill C-90 does nothing for people who have no indexed pension plan, as CN retirees and others know too well.
There is no new policy, no improvement for the thousands upon thousands of Canadian men and women who work for companies without pension plans, the thousands of Canadians who work for small-and medium-size businesses which have no pension plans either, and their future is not made any brighter by these two Bills which we will be considering in the next few days.
Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) must take the blame for this situation. In May of last year, as you may recall, the Minister of Health failed to rise in Cabinet to defend the interests of elderly Canadians and he simply stood by while the old age security pension deindexation project was approved. Elderly Canadians themselves had to march on Parliament Hill on June 19, forcing the Government to recant and admit that the Opposition Parties and retired Canadians were right.
Just looking at the propositions contained in this Bill and in Bill C-90, I can tell they come from the same Minister. There has been some improvement because it was this Minister who sponsored the Bill concerning the spouse's allowance for widows and widowers, but he did not do anything to stop
discrimination against people who are unmarried, separated or divorced, and again we find out that he lacks the leadership and courage to stand up for his own convictions.
I agree with the Minister that negotiating with the provinces is no picnic, but I think these propositions amount to a very minor reform. I sincerely believe that nothing is being done to make sure that all Canadian workers, men and women alike, can look forward to a financially secure retirement. In my opinion, the only groups that stand to gain in this case are the provincial Governments.
Mr. Speaker, let us consider the choices made by this Minister and this Government, let us consider their suggestion that people be allowed to invest in RRSPs to prepare for retirement. I have here an article written by La Presse financial reporter Claude Piche who clearly explains who stands to gain most through RRSPs. Can a man or a woman earning $10,000 afford to invest $1,000, $2,000 or $3,000 in a RRSP for his or her retirement days? No.
Let us refer to the table in Mr. Piche's article. An unmarried taxpayer with a gross income of $10,000 who invests $1,000 in a RRSP will end up with tax savings of $159. Another one whose income is $30,000 and who invests $1,000 in a Registered Retirement Savings Plan will save $347 in taxes. Yet another one who earns $50,000 and invests $1,000 in such a savings plan will pay $432 less in taxes. And if that same person earns $80,000 in Canada, is single and invests $1,000 in a RRSP, it means saving $510.
Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear these measures tend to improve the situation of people who are well off. And how do they affect someone who has been a Member or a Minister here for 15 or 20 years? He will be entitled to his Member's pension. He will be entitled to benefits under the Quebec Pension Plan or the Canada Pension Plan and will be allowed to draw these benefits when he is 60. He won't mind the 5 per cent penalty. He will also have his RRSP and be entitled to this and that and the other. And what do the people in our ridings think about this? There are hundreds of men and women and young people-and I am not talking about people who have already retired. I am talking about people who will retire, eventually. It was hoped that as a result of a thorough reform of our pension system, future generations would not go through what our senior citizens are going through today. We hoped things would be done the way they were done in Europe, in all countries that for over one or two centuries have been concerned about giving people a decent pension plan, a decent retirement plan. Mr. Speaker, we have failed to improve the situation of three quarters of the people in our ridings.
And if we consider all these people who work in a corner store or a grocery store, all these people who work in small businesses? We all know that increasingly, in Canada and Quebec, small business is the industry of the future, but where there are only 10, 15 or 20 employees, there is no provision for a private pension plan, considering the cost and employe earnings.
June 11, 1986

Bill C-90 does not do anything for these people. If we look around in our ridings, none of the people working in the textile and footwear industries, mothers with children, and so forth, have any protection today. We are doing nothing to improve their quality of life. And tomorrow, these people will still have to go and get their Old Age Security pension and their Guaranteed Income Supplement and they will still be living below and on the poverty line. And why is this going to happen? It is because we have not seen fit to take our respon-sabilities seriously.
Mr. Speaker, the Canada Pension Plan is excellent. When they decided to increase contributions they should have made sure that the provinces would repay the money they owe, for the Canada Pension Plan must no longer be a loan fund from which the provinces can borrow at will to pave roads and build sewer systems and highways. That money belongs to working men and women throughout Canada.
Their first objective should have been to make sure that the benefits paid to any Canadian worker from the CPP or the QPP amount to 50 per cent of his or her income. No, Mr. Speaker, the private sector must be left alone, so only one class of people stand to benefit.
There is a three-tier plan in England. The public pension plan is equivalent to what we have in Canada, the old age security pension plan. There is a very important public pension system similar to the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan, and if a company with a collective agreement offers a private pension plan, there is an opting-out option, but people do get decent and reasonable retirement benefits.
I agree there has been some improvement, Mr. Speaker, but unfortunately this same Government in 20 months ... let us keep in mind what it has done to the elderly.
The spouse's allowance, people between 60 and 64, discrimination against 80,000 Canadians, 85 per cent of whom are women, people who are unmarried, separated or divorced, and their civil status is the only reason why they were turned down. The deindexation of old age security pensions: thanks to the elderly, the Government was forced to backtrack and admit it was wrong. Unemployment insurance cut-backs: they brag about making it easier for people to take early retirement. This same Government says: We will allow people aged 60 to 65 to retire early, but there will be a 5 per cent penalty, yet at the same time another Minister states: No way, unemployment insurance benefits will be cut off.
Those are three proposals intended for senior citizens, and as we know home care projects that were offered to provide home care services have been cut, the New Horizons programs, and now they come up with hidden tax increases for future pensioners. Each and every Canadian taxpayer will have to pay more taxes out of his pay cheques, and in return will be entitled to improved benefits if and when disabled. But if the taxpayer does not become disabled, his increased contributions to the Canada Pension Plan will not come back to him as improved benefits, unless he decides to keep working until age
Canada Pension Plan and Federal Court Act
70. Mr. Speaker, we have 1.5 million surplus workers looking for jobs, but this Government is having a policy that encourages people to remain in employment. At the same time, they say: We will let people take early retirement, but if they do so, they will be subject to a 5 per cent penalty. Mr. Speaker, this is inconsistent and ill-concerted. We have the same thing with Bill C-90, and I would like to refer again to the National Welfare Council paper on the poverty level: 50 per cent of senior citizens live below the poverty line. Those between ages 60 and 64 are the less privileged, and the Government intends to increase the percentage of people in that situation by telling them: You are entitled to the Canada Pension Plan, but we are cutting back benefits, you are going to live below the poverty line, and this is what we want. I for one believe the Minister could make another effort before the Bill is adopted. My colleague said he was ready to cooperate and let this Bill pass before the summer recess, but I am wondering if all Hon. Members are doing the right thing. Since we are sure those amendments will not effectively improve the situation for the majority of Canadian men and women, would it not be advisable to ask the Minister to make one more effort and move further amendments. We have in Canada a very efficient communication network-we can use the telephone, make conference calls. We have air travel facilities that allow Ministers to convene. We can use the Hercules. Instead of taking the Minister's family on a junket, we can pick up all the Ministers and have a conference. Sincerely, I feel the Minister could make another effort. I would remind him that last year, in May, he failed to make an extra effort for senior citizens, but senior citizens made that effort and won their day.
If the Minister cannot do anything about the Canada Pension Plan legislation, certainly he can do something about pension reform. Bill C-90, to ensure-and I think that this is what all the Members of this House ultimately want-that the main purpose of any legislation passed to improve Canadian pension plans will be to guarantee that, in the future, no senior citizen will be under the poverty line. We would then need legislation to ensure that these people receive about 50 per cent of their previous income. Otherwise, if we are satisfied with minimal changes simply to improve the standard of living of those who are already well-off, each one of us will have to assume the burden of guilt for letting people live under the poverty line during the next five, ten or fifteen years.
Mr. Speaker, while the spokesmen for the three parties bragged about having done good work and gave us fifteen minutes of mutual compliments, I am convinced that some Members of this House are not completely satisfied with what has been introduced.
Mr. Speaker, for the information of the Hon. Member for Chambly (Mr. Grise), the National Welfare Council is an advisory board appointed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to advise him. The situation is too serious and too important for us not to act to ensure that the thousands of retired Canadians and homemakers will have the decent pension plan which everyone should have in Canada.

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, May 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-75, an Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Maritime Code Act and the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just, before I start my remarks, make a brief intervention by way of a point of order? The Speaker is currently considering a decision taken during report stage of Bill C-75. May I have your indulgence to rise on a point of order at some point later on regarding a matter of procedure?
It gives me a fair amount of pleasure to rise to speak on Bill C-75 at third reading. This Bill has been before us since September of last year. It will amend the Canada Shipping Act, the Arctic Water Pollution Prevention Act, the Maritime Code Act, the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act and a number of consequential Acts as a result of measures included in these amendments.
We have made some important improvements to this Bill during the committee's deliberations at second reading. As I mentioned a moment ago, it is with respect to those amendments that I might want to open a question of procedure later on.
I would first like to compliment the committee and its Chairman, the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), for their very diligent work in the review of this Bill. Over 60 witnesses representing 20 organizations and associations have been heard over the past two or three months. More than 20 amendments were made to the Bill as originally introduced. As a result of the committee's work I believe that we have an improved Bill which will go a long way toward bringing the
Canada Shipping Act into line with similar legislation of our major trading partners around the world.
As I have said on a number of occasions, we have recognized the open-endedness of Clause 4 dealing with the recovery of some portion of Coast Guard expenses. The Minister responded by establishing an appeal process and by embodying principles of fairness and equity in the legislation itself. During his appearance before the committee the Minister advised that it was the intention that Clause 4 would not be proclaimed before January 1, 1987, and that charges for Coast Guard services would not become effective until January of 1988. He also noted that this action would be preceded by an extensive consultation process with Coast Guard stakeholders in major centres across Canada.
The Senate committee hearings are currently in progress. I believe the preconsideration of the Bill was concluded last evening and I think the other Chamber will be moving in concert with us in seeking third reading and passage by the House. In reading the transcripts of the committee hearings I have noted that there still appears to be some misunderstanding with regard to the revenue target set for the introduction of charges under this section of the Canada Shipping Act. I would like to reiterate once again the statements that I and the Minister have made, both within and outside of the Chamber, and to the legislative committee.
I would like to quote statements made to the legislative committee in this regard on March 12, 1986. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) said:
We are looking at something less than 15 per cent, and maybe to be more specific, we will try to quantify that in specific dollar terms. The target in mind would be to realize an additional $20 million net revenue by 1988. That would be commencing in 1988. This would be over and above the forecasted revenue from existing sources of approximately $28 million in 1988-89.
This would have the effect of increasing our revenue to expenditure ratio from the current 3 per cent approximately, to 7 per cent approximately, in net terms, by 1988.
Included in this 7 per cent is revenue forecasted from services which are already subject to cost recovery.
What the Minister has said is quite clear. It is hoped that we can recover an additional $20 million in that time frame. However, that will only increase the percentage from approximately 3 per cent to 7 per cent. As a comparison, approximately 42 per cent of the costs of air transport are now recovered.
It is important for Members to recall that the Auditor General made observations in his reports of March 31, 1983, and March 31, 1985, on cost recovery. He said that cost recovery is an important requirement of the Department's strategic plan. He further stated that the Coast Guard could recover part or all of its cost from users of its services.
There is support for our initiative to recover a small portion-and I emphasize "small"-of Coast Guard expenses. The Council of Boating Organizations of Canada has said that the principle of paying for services is a very legitimate one. Similar expressions of support have come from the Great Lakes Waterway Development Association, the St. Lawrence
June 11, 1986

Ship Owners Association, the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia, the Seafarers International Union, Stelco, Oshawa Harbour Commission, the Dominion Marine Association, and Canada Steamship Lines. I could elaborate, as was done before the committee, but suffice it to say that we are encouraged by the very positive reaction from these important associations, companies and organizations.
I would also note that in committee the exclusion clause for Canadian mobile offshore drilling units drilling on Canada Lands was removed so that the revised Bill provides the enabling legislation for the drafting of regulations to cover Canadian MODUs at all times. The Bill provides that when the regulations for certification and training and for design and construction are submitted for Governor in Council approval, they will be jointly recommended by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney).
You may wish to note that there is precedent for joint recommendation by two Ministers in Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. It is also important to note that drill ships and MODUs are, at one and the same time, floating marine platforms subject to the laws of hydrodynamics as well as industrial sites involved in oil exploration. It is, therefore, appropriate that both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should recommend regulations in this circumstance. We see this, however, as only an interim solution to a very difficult and complex problem.
Pending completion of the comprehensive legislation specific to mobile offshore drilling units announced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on April 14 of this year, a single agency concept was recommended by the royal commission investigating the Ocean Ranger marine disaster. This amendment, proposed by the Government, moved in that direction within the framework of the existing legislation.
I would like to emphasize that this legislation will allow Canada to accede to six international conventions and five codes dealing with certification of masters and seamen, ship construction, ship safety, liability and compensation and prevention and control of pollution from ships. The most important conventions are the conventions for standards of training, certification and watchkeeping for seafarers, the convention for the prevention of pollution from ships, the convention on civil liability for oil pollution damage and the convention on the establishment of an international fund for compensation for oil pollution damage. These codes deal with ships carrying liquified gases in bulk, ships carrying dangerous chemicals and the construction and equipment of mobile offshore drilling units. You will appreciate the importance of this particular piece of legislation as it relates to standards which are international in scope, levels of compensation for damage, and to fines for violation of those provisions.
I would like to talk about certification of pleasure craft operators for a moment. During the course of committee hearings there were very obvious misunderstandings and, as a result, a lot of legitimate apprehension and concern among
Canada Shipping Act
pleasure boat operators. I think a word on that matter is in order. It is our view that these views were erroneously perceived and that there should not be much concern for the people involved. For example, there was great concern that in order to paddle a canoe on a little lake in the woods one had to be a certified operator of a boat, in other words, that one had to have a watchkeeping certificate, that one had to know and understand something about navigation and that one had to know and understand something about engineering. In other words, one has to be something of an expert. That includes your little rowboat, raft, windsurfer, indeed everything. Of course, that is nonsense. That was never the intention at all. In order to reassure the boating public and in response to the concerns expressed by Members and the general public, we amended the Bill to exempt pleasure yachts of less than 20 metres and vessels, boats or craft of any length propelled manually by oars.
Finally, I note that the amendments made during the committee review, taken as a result of strong representations by the Official Opposition, mean that Canada will have stiffer penalties for pollution incidents in our waters. This means that the three existing Part XX penalties of $100,000 will be increased to $200,000. One would be increased to $250,000, and the existing penalty for a Master who does not give reasonable assistance to a pollution prevention officer would be increased from $5,000 to $10,000. If people wonder what I am nodding at, we wondered whether or not the Speaker had ruled these amendments out of order. Apparently they are in order and I am very pleased at that.
The Government gave proof of its willingness to listen to representations made by witnesses and committee members and to react to them in a very positive way. Members of all Parties will understand the importance of this legislation to the shipping community and shipping activity in Canada generally. This Bill significantly improves and modernizes a 50-year old Act dating back to 1936. I urge Members to consider the important safety features fundamental to the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act and recognize the improvements made in this legislation as a result of Bill C-75. For reasons which I believe are evident and in the interests of safe shipping, I ask the House to give expeditious passage to this legislation which has been long awaited both nationally and internationally by the shipping community.

subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the third reading debate on Bill C-75. May I say at the outset as well that I regret I was not here to listen to the words of wisdom from the Parliamentary Secretary at the beginning of his remarks. With his knowledge, consent and co-operation I was with my friend from the NDP ensuring in discussions with the Speaker that these very important amendments to which the Government consented in committee were a legitimate part of this Bill. Those amendments deal with the penalties imposed upon people who knowingly pollute Canada's waters.
Let me begin my remarks by saying to the Parliamentary Secretary that I have found him personally to be extremely cooperative in so far as the examination of this Bill is concerned. I have found the Parliamentary Secretary, personally, to be more than willing and able, on occasion, to ensure that the time required by the legislative committee to examine this Bill was forthcoming and available to us. I have found the Member to be one who has approached many of the amendments of the opposition Parties with an open mind and a fair and reasonable outlook. In fact, in a number of important areas he has responded on occasion to the recommendations not only of the opposition Parties but indeed of members of his Party and members of the general public who have made comments on this Bill. I wanted to state that for the record.
Let me outline some of the more important amendments which were brought to Bill C-75. They include the amendments dealing with the requirement for certification of vessels beyond a certain length, to ensure that not every small boater in this country would find that he was suddenly borne down by the great weight of bureaucratic red tape as represented by this Bill. Another important set of amendments were those dealing with penalties to be imposed on those people who knowingly discharge into Canadian waters pollutants which negatively affect our environment. There are now in place some substantial and stiff penalties. Those were good amendments.
If the Bill dealt primarily with a rewrite of the Canada Shipping Act, which is decades old, if it dealt with excluding small Canadian boaters from bureaucratic red tape, if it dealt with substantially increasing the fines for those who pollute
June 11, 1986

our waters, and if it came to the House in that form only, not only would I be able to say that the Parliamentary Secretary has been co-operative, helpful and reasonable, I would be able to say that he has done a great service to Canadians with this Bill.
However, there is one small problem. Clause 4 is the problem. It is not an amendment of a provision that previously existed in the Act. Clause 4 does not beef up fines that previously existed in the Bill. It is not a change in previous regulations that affected the size of boats. Clause 4 is a new clause that has been introduced despite the screams, the shouts, the protest and reasoned arguments of people who are interested, concerned and knowledgeable about the shipping industry. This clause has been imposed in what otherwise would be a good Bill.
I suppose that the Opposition has two choices. It could say that as far as the Canada Shipping Act and the changes that have been made in the Bill are concerned, it is not a bad Bill and maybe we can ignore this festering sore that the Government has introduced to the Bill.
Our other choice is not to accept what is essentially a good Bill that has been seriously flawed by the Government as a result of its introducing an entirely new measure that heretofor was unheard of. That measure is Clause 4.
My friend from northwestern Ontario asked the Parliamentary Secretary an all too familiar question these days; whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was going to keep his commitment to the Transportation Minister of Quebec, Mr. Cote, and the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa, that he made last week on the CBC national news. That commitment was to re-examine Clause 4 of the Canada Shipping Act before it received final reading in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister told the Quebec Transportation Minister and, more important, the Premier of Quebec: "I will take another look at Clause 4." He said he would take another look at this change which has been thrust upon what otherwise is not a bad Bill. That statement was made a few days ago, but in the House today, when we pick up the latest version of the Bill and look for evidence that the Prime Minister has taken another look, we see Clause 4, unchanged, staring at us from the pages of the Bill.
By now, we are being asked, what is Clause 4? Is it a disease?

subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
My colleague from the New Democratic Party says: "Yes, yes, yes." What is Clause 4? It is an enabling
Canada Shipping Act
provision that gives the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) the power and authority, which he does not and never did have in the history of this country, to impose upon the users of Canada's navigation system charges for services that the Government has always provided as a right to Canadian citizens. It is a provision by which the Minister seeks the authority and power to impose charges on fishermen in Atlantic Canada for Coast Guard services and lifesaving services. They will be charged if they are in danger at sea.
This provision allows the Government to impose charges on all Canadian vessels of every size for icebreaking services everywhere in the country. This provision means that only those who can afford to pay for navigational aids will have them. Therefore, those who live on the bluff of Cape St. George on Port-au-Port Peninsula in the Province of Newfoundland and cannot afford to pay these user fees for navigational aids for search and rescue facilities will not receive them.
This provision allows the Minister of Transport to apply additional user charges for the St. Lawrence Seaway. That is a major mode of transportation which is in decline throughout the Province of Quebec and all Canadian provinces. Those additional user charges may make that transportation system more uneconomic and may put its very future in doubt, thereby choking the life from that major Canadian transportation artery.
If that is not bad enough, let me tell the House what is worse. Not only does the Minister of Transport want the power to impose all these charges on the people of Canada, he will not tell us who will be charged, how much and for how long, until later. When one hands someone a gun and that person says he wants the hammer pulled back and the bullet shoved into the breech, is it not logical to ask for whom the bullet is intended, and why? The Minister, asking for the authority to impose charges through Clause 4, is asking for a loaded gun. It is a user-pay concept, as my colleague, the Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) points out. The Minister wants the gun and the ammunition but he will only tell us we are the targets after we get the bullet right between the eyes.
The Government, in asking for this authority, made no reference in this 111-page Bill to who will be charged, how much and how these charges will affect their economic wellbeing.
The Government has done absolutely no analysis of the impact on the St. Lawrence Seaway. It has done no analysis to find out whether fishermen in the Gaspe of Quebec, in Shediac, New Brunswick, White Bay, Newfoundland, in South West Nova or along the coast of British Columbia can afford these additional charges. I see Hon. Members opposite from fishing constituencies. I know that short of Party discipline and the threat of the Party Whip being laid across their backs, they would be on their feet in outrage that such a regressive

June 11, 1986
Canada Shipping Act
measure would be imposed upon their constituents. I empathize with those Hon. Members as much as I do with the fishermen.
I am sure the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) is a Minister who is congnizant of the fact that the fishermen in the area of the Great Northern Peninsula had a summer storm yesterday which rolled in over an area of 100 miles and wiped out their lobster traps, destroyed their gear and took away their means of livelihood. I am sure he is aware that those fishermen are not comfortable with the notion that the Minister of Transport has been given a gun, that it has been loaded and it is pointed at them. They do not know whether they can carry on their backs, on top of a poor fishery-better prices but poor landings this year, as the Minister is aware-the provisions of this Bill.
The Minister is so unsure of the political reception this Bill is going to receive that he says he will tell us about it a year from now. After he has been given the gun he will tell us a year from now who is to be shot with it. The fishermen of Atlantic Canada and British Columbia have already had one shot through the bow and they are taking on water.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans himself is imposing berthing fees for the first time in the history of Atlantic Canada. He is going to charge a fisherman to tie up to a wharf. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, such a ludicrous proposition? The Government of Canada has a wharf. Tied to the wharf are 10 vessels going out in a straight line. The wharf is only big enough for one boat to tie up to it. The question becomes, who pays the berthing fee? Is it Tom who is tied up to the wharf, or Bob who is tied up to Tom, or Harry who is tied up to Bob? The Minister is going to impose the wharfage fee because he has had a $100 million shameful and shocking cut-back in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. That is the issue.
We cannot look at Clause 4 of this Bill in isolation. The provisions of Clause 4, even though it is a Bill of the Minister of Transport, will apply to the constituency of the Minister of Fisheries. They will apply to the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) because the potato farmers in Prince Edward Island are being told that if they want to move their potatoes to market, and if there is an ice problem, the Government will send in an ice-breaker but the potato farmers will pay for the ice-breaking costs. Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? If a farmer grows potatoes where there is ice, he will pay an extra charge. If a farmer happens to live in the interior of this country, and not on the Atlantic Coast, he does not have to carry those kinds of charges. We are going to have first and second class Canadian farmers based on this Bill. Those who live in areas where the Government is expected to provide ice-breaking services are second class Canadians, according to this Bill. But if a farmer happens to live in the central region of the country by the railroad lines-we do not have one in Newfoundland, at least for a few more days-or if he happens
to live near a trans-Canada Highway, there is no problem, it is gratis, compliments of the Government of Canada. But if he happens to be clinging to the rock on the edge of the Atlantic Ocean trying to scrape a living out of an area where unemployment is high and opportunities are few, then, by God, we bring down the hammer and slap another charge on his back. I see the Hon. Member from Port aux Basques sitting opposite. He is nodding his head in agreement.
I intend to talk a little more about Clause 4. But as an introduction to some of the kinds of things which bother me about what could have been a good piece of legislation, I would like to speak about another major flaw in this Bill. A major recommendation of the $15 million royal commission, established jointly between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland to look into the Ocean Ranger disaster, was to include within Bill C-75 provision for bringing oil rigs which operate off Canada's East Coast, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, under the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. That was a recommendation of the $15 million royal commission co-sponsored by both Governments which looked into the February 15, 1982, sinking of the Ocean Ranger, which was a disaster regretted by all Members from all Parties. It resulted in the loss of the entire crew of that vessel, 84 men, including 69 Canadians, 56 of whom were from my home Province of Newfoundland. That is a disaster which none of us wants repeated, and a great deal has been done to improve the conditions in the offshore. There is no question about that. A great deal has been done by this administration and by the previous administration.
The major cause identified by the royal commission studying the disaster was inadequate training and inadequate command structure. The solution was to include those rigs under the Canada Shipping Act. It was recommended not to leave them out there in limbo under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. That recommendation has been ignored in Bill C-75, nothwithstanding the fact that the Liberal Party in committee moved amendments to this Bill to include those rigs under the jurisdiction of the Canada Shipping Act. Those amendments were defeated by the unanimous, negative, no vote of Members of the Progressive Conservative Party.
I take this opportunity to thank my colleague in the New Democratic Party who at least saw the wisdom and voted for the amendments I had the pleasure of moving on behalf of my Party. The Royal Commission on the Ocean Ranger Marine Disaster indicated in its report that the main contributing factor to the breakdown of the command structure on board the vessel was the fact that the captain who commanded the oil ring, when the rig and crew were in danger, did not have the proper qualifications to avoid what transpired. That was on February 18, 1982. Today, as we in this House debate the provisions of Bill C-75, we are aware that still today six rigs operate in the offshore of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, four in Newfoundland and four in Nova Scotia. Those rigs still do not have the command structure in place. They do not have

a barge used for cargo was a ship, using the definition found in the Canada Shipping Act.
So according to the Canadian courts a barge which moves primarily all types of products with no humans on board is a ship and therefore falls under the jurisdiction of the Canada Shipping Act. A floating crane which operates primarily in harbour and not out 200 miles in the stormy and savage North Atlantic is also a ship. There is no problem there. However, an oil rig, which the Federal Court has decided is a ship under the Canada Shipping Act, is not a ship. It is there as part of a personal kingdom, one of the emperor's toys under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Energy. This is so notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Transport knows better, as does his Parliamentary Secretary, who is honest enough to admit he knows it. This is so notwithstanding the fact that if a free vote were taken in the House, every Member would say: "For God's sake, man, let's do the right and intelligent thing". For some reason or another the Minister of Energy, for her own political, egotistical reasons, has been able to keep out of the Canada Shipping Act the recommendations of a royal commission primarily designed to prevent a repeat of a disaster
which all of us regret and which all of us would not want to see happen again. It is for those reasons that I cannot support this Bill at third reading.
